newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gensec sees robust SAfrica industrials, bonds.
newsitem.headline: Gensec sees robust SAfrica industrials, bonds.

text.p: South African industrial shares and long bonds look set for a robust performance in the next six months buoyed by foreign investment inflows, Genbel Securities Ltd (Gensec) said on Monday.

But this optimism was dependent on the rand not repeating its dismal performance of last year when it lost 29 percent of its value against the dollar, Anton Botha, chief executive of the South African investment group, said.

Gensec released first half results for the period to end-December 1996 showing a massive 92 percent surge in earnings to 102 cents a share with underwriting activities contributing the lion's share of profits.
The group expected this strong six month performance to be repeated in the second half provided there was no marked deterioration in local investment markets.
"The interest rate and equity markets should be good," Botha told Reuters in an interview.

He said the liquidity which has driven U.S. and European bourses to record levels in the past six months was unlikely to dry up and some may be diverted into Johannesburg shares which were relatively cheap after a flat performance in 1996.
"Those markets (U.S. and European) are becoming quite expensive so I think there is going to be a spillover into the emerging markets of which we are part," Botha said.
He said the IFC Emerging Markets Index, which tracked a dull performance for most emerging countries last year, had turned up sharply in January, led mainly by gains on the Russian market.
"And those sort of things spill over to you," Botha said.
Over the 1996 year the Johannesburg Stock Exchange's industrial index dipped less than one percent.

Gensec is active in securities trading, treasury operations, financial engineering and risk management, with its biggest exposure being to the equity market. The firm is keen in the long term to increase its exposure towards interest rates.

South African bonds were also starting to look more attractive after a poor showing in 1996 as high yields seen last year in countries including Spain, Portugal and Italy, toppled off their peaks, Botha said.
"The guys that chase yields have fewer and fewer places to chase. So we must become more attractive to them...and hopefully we will suck in some foreign money."
The yield on South Africa's key long bond, the R150, rose almost 200 basis points in 1996 to end above 16 percent.
But the rand, which has since the beginning of the year retraced over five percent of last year's losses, remained the one wild card threatening to unsettle upbeat market forecasts.

"The problem is that while we have exchange controls, there is always a question mark whether the rand is correctly valued. Any little problem that comes around can lead to uncertainty around the rand," Botha said.
"Until we have lifted exchange controls it will always remain the bogeyman in the cabinet. It remains the one thing that could unsettle the market for us."

Commenting on an announcement on Friday that Gensec was considering making an offer to minority shareholders in Randex Ltd, Botha said a buyout of the mining rights company would free up cash, which lay dormant until a mining opportunity came up.
Gensec owns a 64.57 percent stake in Randex which Botha said was valued at 130 million rand.

"There is a large amount of value sitting inside Randex which is earmarked exclusively for mining operations. If we can bring the money inside Gensec then we can deploy the money where it is needed," Botha said. -- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
